Cushy
KUSH-ee
adjective (Silent Generation slang)
British Army slang of the First World War, recorded from 1915, from Hindi and Urdu khush (pleasant, happy), picked up by soldiers who had served in India. A cushy job was a soft, safe posting. The word crossed into American use and was common in the service by the 1940s; it has stayed in everyday speech for any easy, comfortable situation.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In the service, everyone wanted a cushy job — a desk in a rear area, a posting far from the shooting, a sergeant who did not care much. After the war the word came home: a cushy job pays well and asks little. Wanting a little ease is not wicked; the Lord gives His people rest. Jesus Himself said, "my yoke is easy, and my burden is light" (Mat 11:30). But Scripture warns about loving ease more than duty. The prophet thundered, "Woe to them that are at ease in Zion" (Amo 6:1) — people comfortable while the nation fell apart. Jesus told of a rich man who said to himself, "Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry" (Luk 12:19). That night God called him a fool, and his soul was required of him. Paul told young Timothy to expect the opposite of cushy: "Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ" (2Ti 2:3). And Paul himself, who had known prisons and shipwrecks, wrote, "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content" (Php 4:11). The Christian does not hunt for the cushy post. He takes the post God gives, easy or hard, and is content in it. And he knows that the easy yoke Christ offers was bought at the hardest price: the Lord took no cushy road, but the road to the cross.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (British Army WWI, from Hindi khush; common in 1940s American service) for an easy, comfortable job or posting — ease Scripture permits but warns against loving (Amo 6:1), calling us to contentment in any state.

expand to see more

CUSHY, adj. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s; British Army from 1915, from Hindi khush) Easy, comfortable, undemanding, of a job or posting. "He landed a cushy job in the quartermaster’s office."

Decode for families: cushy means easy — fine to enjoy, dangerous to love more than duty.

Key Scripture

Mat 11:30 — "For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light."

Amo 6:1 — "Woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria, which are named chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel came!"

Luk 12:19 — "And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry."

2Ti 2:3 — "Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ."

Php 4:11 — "Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content."

Modern Corruption

A neutral word for comfort; the snare is the love of ease that dodges duty and settles down while others bear the load.

expand to see more

There is no sin in a comfortable job, and Scripture never calls ease evil in itself; rest is God’s gift. A grandfather who finally landed a cushy job after hard years earned it honestly.

The danger is in the seeking. The man whose chief aim is the cushy post will dodge hard duty, leave the heavy work to others, and grow at ease in Zion (Amo 6:1). Scripture puts contentment in its place (Php 4:11): take what God gives, work it faithfully, and do not make comfort your god.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hindi/Urdu khush (pleasant) → 1915 British Army cushy (soft, safe) → 1940s American service slang → everyday "easy, comfortable."
